idiom_name: narrow catch/discard around the single call, with a written justification
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: isolate the one call inside the language's suppression construct - catch a named failure type with an empty handler, discard a Result/error value explicitly, or use a stdlib suppression helper - and keep the construct to that one call so failures of everything else still travel to the caller. Put the justification next to it: which failure values the call can produce and why each is inconsequential. Where the language offers a non-failing form of the same operation (a TryX API, a non-throwing overload, a presence check before the delete), prefer it over the mute. If the ignored failure has diagnostic value, leave a debug-level breadcrumb instead of discarding it silently.
code_sketch:
# narrow: only this call, only this failure type
with suppress(SpecificError):        # why: '<documented, inconsequential condition>'
    best_effort_call()
# everything else still propagates:
result = other_call()                # not muted
pitfalls: Widening the swallow to the language's root error type (Throwable, Exception, StandardError, bare rescue) turns the idiom into the blanket-catch anti-pattern.
Wrapping more than the single call also hides failures of statements that were never analysed for ignorability.
An ignore whose justification cannot be re-checked - no documented contract and no test - is a comment, not a proof, and it decomposes silently on the next refactor.
An explicit Rust `let _ =` or Go `errors.Is(..., fs.ErrNotExist)` check is not a generic error sink: match only the documented case and preserve escalation for every other failure.
